title: Probability Judgment in Artificial Intelligence
extended_summary:
This paper examines two approaches to probability judgment in artificial intelligence: Bayesian probability and the theory of belief functions (also called Dempster-Shafer theory). Its central concern is how these approaches differ as languages for representing uncertainty, especially when evidence is incomplete or does not fit neatly into a full probabilistic model. Shafer frames the discussion around constructive probability, arguing that probability judgments depend on how evidence is mapped onto canonical examples rather than on a single normative calculus.

The paper illustrates the distinction with simple examples involving testimony, thermometer evidence, and dependent versus independent sources of evidence. In the belief-function approach, probability is first modeled over evidence or related questions and then extended to the target question; in Bayesian analysis, probabilities are modeled more directly over the answer to the question and its conditioning evidence. The examples show that belief functions can be more convincing when one cannot justify all the probabilistic judgments required by a Bayesian design, especially when evidence is partial or when dependence structures are hard to specify.

The latter part of the paper discusses the relevance of these ideas for expert systems in artificial intelligence. Shafer argues that belief functions offer greater modularity than full Bayesian designs and can be easier to use in rule-based systems such as MYCIN-like expert systems. However, he also emphasizes that neither approach fully captures human probability judgment, which depends on the ability to design probability arguments as well as compute them. The paper concludes that both Bayesian and belief-function methods have niches in AI, but that the deeper challenge is developing flexible methods for designing probability models.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/theoretical paper on probability judgment in AI and expert systems, not an empirical K-12 study. It presents illustrative examples and arguments rather than a clear research design, sample, or outcome evaluation.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper does not report educational intervention effects, student outcomes, or K-12 science inquiry evidence. It has no measurable impact estimate relevant to the requested topic of AI-powered science inquiry supports in K-12.
